personal.name: Agrim Sigdel
personal.summary:
I am a Full-Stack Developer and published AI researcher specializing in building end-to-end machine learning pipelines and the robust web infrastructure required to scale them. My focus lies at the intersection of applied artificial intelligence and scalable software architecture.

I have a proven track record of designing advanced computer vision architectures (YOLO, RT-DETR) and deploying them into production-ready SaaS platforms using Python/Django, React, and AWS. Whether I am architecting a multi-tenant CRM, optimizing a React Native mobile application for high performance, or engineering a cascaded AI vision pipeline that reduces compute load by over 60%, I am driven by the challenge of turning complex theoretical frameworks into user-centric, high-availability tools.

projects.title: Feriaau
projects.outcome: A production platform shared by the web experience and Feriaau’s mobile apps.

caseStudy.tagline: Giving each shop its own loyalty programme, without building a separate system for every shop.
caseStudy.role: Full-Stack Engineer — backend services, REST APIs, frontend, server configuration, CI/CD
highlights: Shared APIs for web and mobile

sections.heading: What I worked on
sections.body:
Feriaau brings catalogues, orders, points, coupons, and rewards into one platform. I worked across the Django backend, the React frontend, and the server and release setup.

The important detail is that a customer earns points with a particular shop. That relationship runs through the whole product: the balance they see, the rewards they can claim, and what a member of staff is allowed to change.

sections.heading: What the platform covers
sections.body:
The customer side connects vendor discovery and product catalogues with carts, orders, points, coupons, gift cards, and rewards. The vendor side brings the shop’s catalogue, customers, orders, and loyalty activity into one workspace. Customer drilldowns make it possible to look beyond the summary numbers.

There are separate user, vendor, administrator, and superadmin routes. Onboarding, email verification, vendor access, trials, and permissions determine which parts of that workspace someone can use. Reporting includes customer analytics, QR activity, and loyalty performance; notifications and the POS integration support the work around those screens.

The screenshots focus on the public entry point and two vendor views. The wider feature scope comes from the application routes and backend domains, rather than implying that every module is visible in those three images.

sections.heading: Getting the boundaries right
sections.body:
I kept the backend as a modular Django application, with separate domains for things like orders, points, and users. A points balance belongs to a customer and a vendor, and transactions are recorded separately so there is a history behind the number on screen.

The API also uses a shared response format. That made the React side easier to work with: errors and successful responses follow the same contract across features. Permission classes handle common rules such as whether a vendor is active.

sections.heading: Working with another system
sections.body:
The Atithi POS integration needed room to change as its API evolved. I kept the mapping between the two systems in a separate integration app instead of spreading external IDs through the core models.

Status mappings and per-flow switches live in configuration. Outgoing work runs through Celery, and incoming webhooks are logged. That gives support a record to investigate and lets us pause an integration without stopping the rest of the platform.

sections.heading: What shipped
sections.body:
The platform has a staging environment and a separate production release step. I also documented the setup, application flow, and extension points for the next developer.

The walkthrough combines the public site with local captures of the vendor dashboard and customer drilldown. Sample records keep the operational screens readable without exposing customer accounts.

projects.title: peeq
projects.outcome: A working storefront and try-on experience, with vendor tools still in development.

caseStudy.tagline: A little look before you buy: bringing virtual try-on into the way local shops sell clothes.
highlights: Shopfront, product page, and try-on kiosk
Fabric and cut previews for tailoring shops

sections.heading: What I’m building
sections.body:
peeq starts with a small shopping question: how might this look on me? A shopper picks a piece from a store and enters a try-on flow. The shop gets a catalogue, a storefront, and a kiosk it can use in person.

I’m the founder and full-stack engineer. The work spans the shopper experience, the shop dashboard, the AI integration, and the operational tools behind them.

sections.heading: The experience beyond try-on
sections.body:
For shoppers, the product includes store discovery, individual storefronts, garment pages, kiosk entry, QR links, saved account views, and comparison. A shop can use the catalogue online or bring the same experience to its counter.

The repository also contains owner and shop dashboards, fabric tooling, and administration for shops, users, billing, and operations. These are different audiences with different jobs: showing a garment, maintaining a shop, and running the platform.

The captures follow the public shopping flow. They do not demonstrate a completed AI generation, payment, or private administration session. Those parts should be assessed separately from the storefront walkthrough.

sections.heading: The part behind the preview
sections.body:
The Next.js server handles generation requests so provider keys stay off the client. A repeat request can reuse a cached result, and usage checks happen before a paid call. Shop allowances are reserved before generation and refunded when a request fails.

I also built a local storage adapter for demonstrations. The catalogue and interface can work without the hosted database; generating a new AI result still needs a connection. That distinction matters when showing the product in a shop.

sections.heading: When there is no product photo
sections.body:
Tailoring adds a different problem: the finished garment may not exist yet. I modelled fabrics and cuts separately so a shop can preview a combination before it is made.

A fabric photo cannot describe everything. The studio also carries notes about details such as borders and drape. These previews help explain a proposed piece; they are not a promise of exact fit or fabric behaviour.

sections.heading: Where it stands
sections.body:
The public storefront and try-on entry are available, and the wider product is still in development. The walkthrough follows a real product from the public catalogue into its kiosk.

The shopper-facing page currently hands order confirmation, payment, and delivery back to the shop. Those handoffs are part of the current shopping flow.

projects.title: Partweave
projects.outcome: An open-source scaffolder that generates code you own, with a plan step before it writes files.

caseStudy.tagline: Choose the pieces of a stack, check how they fit, and start with a repository you can own.
highlights: Add modules to an existing scaffold

sections.heading: Why I built it
sections.body:
Setting up a full-stack project involves a lot of familiar work: an API, a client, authentication, environment files, and local services. I built Partweave to make that setup reusable while still letting me choose which parts belong in a project.

The generated application does not depend on Partweave at runtime. Once it is written, it is ordinary source code.

sections.heading: What is built, and what is still planned
sections.body:
The current module catalogue includes PostgreSQL, authentication, storage, Docker, CI, a web UI kit, a working client–server example, and feedback forms. Storage supplies local and S3 adapters; feedback can connect the server, web, and mobile apps without requiring authentication.

The CLI supports planning before generation, inspecting the catalogue, creating a project, and adding modules later. Module contracts and generated-project checks are part of that workflow, because a selectable module needs to work with its declared dependencies.

Role-based access, rate limiting, audit logging, and the workflow engine are documented plans. They are kept outside the selectable module catalogue until they are implemented and tested. This distinction is important when describing what someone can install today.

sections.heading: Deciding what fits together
sections.body:
Each module describes what it needs and what it provides. Authentication can require a database capability without naming one particular database module. The resolver expands those requirements and rejects conflicting combinations before generation.

Optional wiring is applied after the full module set is resolved. That keeps the output from changing just because modules were visited in a different order.

sections.heading: A deliberately simple way to edit files
sections.body:
Modules insert lines at named anchor comments in the scaffolds. The same approach works across Python, TypeScript, configuration files, and Dockerfiles, and skips lines that are already present.

The trade-off is visible: removing an anchor can break a later addition. I chose that constraint over maintaining a separate syntax transformer for every language in the stack.

sections.heading: What is available
sections.body:
Partweave is published on npm with commands for creating, planning, inspecting, and extending projects. The supported framework choices are Django, Next.js, and Expo; arbitrary framework combinations are outside the current scope.

The most useful part of the project for me has been working out the module contract. It gives new components a predictable way to participate without teaching the generator about each one individually.

projects.title: easy-3dkit
projects.outcome: A published npm package used by this portfolio’s terminal backdrop.

caseStudy.tagline: The 3D setup I kept needing, turned into reusable React components.
highlights: A published package used in this portfolio

sections.heading: What I wanted to make easier
sections.body:
A background effect can require a surprising amount of setup: a canvas, camera, input handling, resize behaviour, and a fallback when WebGL is unavailable. easy-3dkit packages that common work so I can start with a Stage and compose components inside it.

I built the library and its gallery together. The gallery is a place to try the components, adjust their controls, and copy a useful starting point.

sections.heading: How the pieces fit together
sections.body:
Stage handles the scene setup. InteractiveSurface and its materials cover shader-based surfaces, while InstancedGrid and its layouts handle repeated geometry. Pointer-driven behaviour and shared utilities let those components participate in an interactive page.

The gallery adds controls and copyable examples around the components. The package also includes a starter workflow and an optional post-processing entry point. Server rendering, missing WebGL support, resizing, and package exports are part of the integration work behind the visual demo.

The walkthrough shows the documentation and one live effect. It introduces the component families and the path to using them; it is not a screenshot catalogue of every variant.

sections.heading: One component, different looks
sections.body:
An InteractiveSurface takes a material; an InstancedGrid takes a layout. Changing that input changes the visual while the component keeps responsibility for its lifecycle and rendering.

The variant types and shared shader utilities are public extension points. A user can make a new material without having to fork the whole component.

sections.heading: The less visible work
sections.body:
Packaging needed as much care as the effects. The 3D engine is a peer dependency so a consuming application can share its existing copy. Optional post-processing has its own entry point.

I also added checks around the built package and starter. Building the documentation against the distribution catches missing exports and packaging mistakes that source imports would hide.

sections.heading: Using it outside its own repo
sections.body:
This portfolio installs easy-3dkit as a dependency and uses it for the terminal backdrop. That gives me another place to find integration problems.

The library is still pre-1.0. I’m treating the public API, fallback behaviour, and release process as part of the product, alongside the effects you can see.

projects.title: Kingsoft CRM
projects.outcome: A CRM for Feriaau’s operations, with the tenant boundaries and their limitations documented.

caseStudy.tagline: Keeping contacts, deals, and follow-ups organised across separate teams.

sections.heading: The job of the CRM
sections.body:
The CRM brings together contacts, deals, tasks, tickets, meetings, and finance records. Several organisations use the same deployment, so every business record needs a clear owner and every request needs the right organisation context.

I worked on the Django backend and the interface, including the shared infrastructure for permissions and record handling.

sections.heading: The full organisation workspace
sections.body:
The default Workspace menu contains Dashboard, Contacts, Deals, Tasks, Tickets, Meetings, and Analytics. Contacts include search, stage and owner filters, imports, exports, and custom fields. Deals can be viewed as a table or a pipeline board; the other modules cover follow-up work, support requests, appointments, and reporting.

Finance exposes Commissions. The Organization section contains General Settings, Organization Defaults, Team Members, Audit Log, Billing, and API Keys. Help Center and Support complete the navigation. These are the 16 organisation menu entries in the source’s default sidebar.

Visibility depends on role and permission. The captures use an Owner fixture to show the organisation’s full default menu. The sidebar scrolls independently, so the later capture shows the settings and support entries below the workspace links.

sections.heading: Platform administration is a separate role
sections.body:
Superadmins have four default navigation entries: Platform Settings, Organization Approvals, Sidebar Control, and Role Permission Control. Their role is to administer the platform, so the application gives them a separate navigation view from an organisation member.

Sidebar Control manages sections, links, ordering, and actions as data. Role Permission Control governs the access rules behind those entries. The menu is therefore both configurable and permission-aware; showing every entry to every account would misrepresent how the CRM works.

The final screenshot uses the original Sidebar Control interface with the source’s seeded menu definitions. It demonstrates the platform view without connecting to a live organisation or changing its configuration.

sections.heading: Keeping the interface close to Django
sections.body:
The interface uses Django templates and a JavaScript fragment loader. The app shell stays in place while page fragments change. That suited a product built largely from forms and tables and kept the rendering close to the server-side permission context.

It also meant maintaining our own table, dialog, and board behaviour. That is a cost of the approach, even when the server-side integration is convenient.

sections.heading: Deletion has to respect relationships
sections.body:
Hiding a parent record is only part of soft deletion. Its related records still need a consistent outcome. I built a deletion pass that collects the affected records, checks protected relationships before writing, and then applies the cascade or null behaviour.

That work is less visible than a dashboard, but it matters when someone deletes a contact or another record with a long history attached.

sections.heading: What I checked along the way
sections.body:
I reviewed how organisation context was resolved during an authentication change and documented places where the paths differed. Organisation isolation relies on those application-level checks, so inconsistencies in the request path needed particular attention.

The walkthrough uses the actual Django templates with fictional contacts. It shows the day-to-day interface while keeping real operational records out of the portfolio.

projects.title: ANPR + Smart Parking System
projects.outcome: A research-backed prototype for camera-based parking sessions, with stage metrics reported separately from end-to-end estimates.

caseStudy.tagline: Reading a small licence plate in a busy camera frame, one stage at a time.
highlights: 97.1% / 97.8% test mAP@50 for plate / character stages
Parking sessions around the recognition pipeline

sections.heading: Starting with the camera frame
sections.body:
A parking camera sees much more than a licence plate. The plate may be small, reflective, or partly obscured, and Nepali plates bring both Devanagari and Latin characters into the task.

I split recognition into three stages: find the vehicle, find the plate inside that crop, then read the characters. This became the validation case for my Cascaded AI Task Decomposition research.

sections.heading: The operator workflow around the model
sections.body:
The dashboard connects camera feeds and detections with parking sessions. Operators can inspect activity, enter a plate manually when recognition needs help, and review entry and exit records. Pricing and reporting sit alongside that operational workflow.

The project also has image and video input paths for examining recognition outside a live camera stream. Tracking and cached reads reduce repeated inference, while error reporting gives a place to investigate failed processing.

The dashboard, session list, and manual-entry captures use a local fixture API with DEMO plates. Their sample totals and percentages illustrate the interface; they are separate from the research measurements described below.

sections.heading: Why the stages are separate
sections.body:
YOLOv8n filters frames for vehicles. A trained YOLOv11n model locates the plate, and RF-DETR Base detects the characters. Each stage passes a smaller region to the next, reducing the background the recogniser has to deal with.

In the parking prototype, tracking and a cache tie a plate read to a vehicle across frames. A car staying in view should not trigger a fresh OCR request for every frame.

sections.heading: What the evaluation says
sections.body:
The paper reports held-out test mAP@50 of 97.1% for plate localisation and 97.8% for character recognition. These are stage detection metrics, not the percentage of complete plates read correctly.

The 90.4% end-to-end precision figure is a model-based estimate formed from stage precisions. Errors can be correlated across stages, so a direct full-string benchmark is still needed. The dataset also has limited coverage for rare characters.

sections.heading: Connecting recognition to parking
sections.body:
The surrounding application uses FastAPI and a Next.js dashboard for cameras, detections, sessions, and pricing. Entry and exit detections feed the session workflow.

Hosted inference can fail, so the stream and inference paths have to degrade separately. The result is a prototype that connects the research to an operational flow; it should not be read as a validated unattended billing system.

projects.title: Reddit Sentiment Analysis
projects.outcome: A seven-emotion view of posts and communities, with aggregation that accounts for different comment volumes.

caseStudy.tagline: Looking at the emotions in a community without simply measuring how busy it is.
highlights: Server batch jobs and browser inference

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body:
The app analyses text, Reddit posts, and whole subreddits into emotion distributions. It also stores repeated community analyses so they can be compared over time.

My work was in the application, inference pipeline, and aggregation. The classifiers are existing models; I did not train or fine-tune the shipped models.

sections.heading: From one input to a community comparison
sections.body:
A user can begin with a piece of text, a Reddit post, or a subreddit. Longer jobs report progress while they run. The result views break down the sampled text and comments into emotion scores, rather than reducing the output to one positive-or-negative label.

Stored analyses support a community history, a sortable leaderboard, and CSV export. Scheduled and interactive work share the analysis pipeline, while the browser model provides another path for direct text exploration.

The walkthrough shows the input page and the real leaderboard template populated with fictional communities. It explains the queue and aggregation flow separately; no inference run or real community result is claimed by those screenshots.

sections.heading: Two ways to run the model
sections.body:
Longer Reddit jobs run in a Celery worker behind Flask. For interactive text, a second model runs in a browser Web Worker through Transformers.js and WebAssembly. Its weights load when that path is selected.

The two engines return the same seven-category interface, but they use different models and label mappings. A matching chart shape does not make their scores directly comparable.

sections.heading: Fixing what the leaderboard measured
sections.body:
Adding predictions together made larger communities score higher on every emotion. That was measuring activity as much as mood. I changed aggregation to use distributions and weighted means at the post level, then averages across posts.

I also kept text cleaning conservative. Punctuation, casing, and emoji can carry useful context for the model, even though they do not have one fixed emotional meaning.

sections.heading: Keeping inference out of the web process
sections.body:
The web app queues work; the worker loads and runs the classifier. Moving model construction behind lazy accessors stopped ordinary web workers from loading weights they never used.

The project supports English text and inherits the limitations of its models, including sarcasm and context. Its scores are a way to explore language in the sampled posts, not a diagnosis of the people writing them.

projects.title: ContractorOps AI App
projects.outcome: A mobile application in active development, with shared handling for authentication, requests, and connectivity failures.

caseStudy.tagline: Helping contractors work through leads, quotes, and projects from a phone.

sections.heading: My part of the project
sections.body:
ContractorOps AI brings leads, quotes, proposals, project details, and crew work into a mobile app. I’m responsible for the React Native application and its API integration, working with a FastAPI backend.

A field workflow has to account for interrupted connections. That made request behaviour and recovery part of the interface work from the start.

sections.heading: What the mobile app brings together
sections.body:
The feature modules cover leads, clients, follow-ups, quotes, proposals, and invoices. Projects, crew, tasks, work, and calendar screens support the handoff from winning a job to delivering it.

Assistant, lead-generation, frontline, integration, reporting, and settings modules extend that core flow. My work is on the mobile screens, shared behaviour, and API integration; the presence of a module in the repository does not mean every connected service has been exercised in this walkthrough.

The three images below are from the project’s existing interactive design prototype: the overview, quote list, and proposal detail. They explain the intended journey. They are clearly labelled because they are not screenshots of a running native build.

sections.heading: Getting startup and sessions right
sections.body:
The app waits for stored authentication and fonts before mounting its main navigation. Tokens are mirrored in memory after startup so every request does not have to read secure storage again.

When several requests encounter an expired token, they share one refresh operation. That avoids a burst of competing refresh calls. A failed refresh clears the session instead of keeping the app in a retry loop.

sections.heading: Making failures understandable
sections.body:
The request client normalises errors so screens receive a consistent shape. Network and server failures can retry; validation failures need a useful message and a changed input.

Connectivity state is connected to the query layer, with an offline banner and a shared toast surface. A root error boundary handles rendering failures. These cover different failures rather than treating every problem as the same retry button.

sections.heading: Keeping it maintainable
sections.body:
Routes declare navigation while feature modules hold the screens and logic. Shared controls separate behaviour from themed rendering, so loading, disabled states, and accessibility do not have to be reimplemented on every screen.

This is client work in active development. The visual walkthrough uses the interactive prototype already in the repository. It shows the intended product flow while the native app continues to develop.

caseStudy.tagline: Bringing the loyalty programme to the customer’s phone and the shop counter.

sections.heading: Two audiences, two apps
sections.body:
Customers need to find a vendor, check their points, and redeem rewards. Staff need a different view of orders and the work at the counter. Feriaau handles those audiences through separate Flutter apps over the same backend.

I contributed feature UI and API integration to the consumer app with the wider mobile team, and built the vendor companion. The consumer application was shared team work.

sections.heading: What each app is responsible for
sections.body:
The consumer journey starts with finding a vendor, opening its page, and checking the points attached to that relationship. Rewards, coupons, QR scanning, and notifications support the return visit. The published screenshots show discovery, a vendor page, and the points balance.

The vendor companion has its own authentication, home, order, and notification features. Its purpose is to support staff work rather than reproduce every consumer screen. Both apps rely on the same platform services, but each has its own presentation and state.

The images here document the published consumer experience. The vendor companion is explained from its source and architecture; no consumer screenshot is presented as a vendor screen.

sections.heading: A structure we could share
sections.body:
Both applications separate feature presentation from the data access behind it. Pages work through BLoCs or Cubits and repository interfaces; core services own concerns such as HTTP, persistence, and routing.

That made it easier to work across the two apps. The vendor app uses generated dependency registrations, while the older consumer app has manual registrations.

sections.heading: The details around everyday use
sections.body:
Token storage, refresh, and request interception have separate responsibilities. The consumer app also includes QR scanning, local caching, notifications, and update prompts.

One useful change was replacing a Flutter-rendered splash with the native splash. The operating system can show that before the Flutter engine starts, avoiding the blank period that an in-app animation cannot cover.

sections.heading: What shipped
sections.body:
The consumer app is published on Google Play and the App Store. The screenshots here come from its public App Store listing and show the consumer experience.

Automated coverage is still an area to improve. The separate repositories and state layers give me a useful starting point for that work.

highlights: A terminal with a virtual filesystem
3D loaded when the terminal needs it

sections.heading: Why there are three ways in
sections.body:
Some visitors want a quick account of my experience. Others want to look through the projects or try something interactive. I built a CV view, a visual portfolio, and a terminal so the same work can be explored in different ways.

All three read the same content tree. The generated résumé reads it too, which reduces the places I have to edit when something changes.

sections.heading: What visitors and editors can do
sections.body:
Visitors can read the CV, browse the visual project collection, or explore the terminal. Project pages add the problem, my contribution, implementation choices, limitations, and a visual walkthrough. Images open at a larger size for a closer look.

The terminal offers content navigation and scene controls, while the résumé generation reuses the same profile data. Contact, metadata, and offline-support work sit around those main views.

The editor manages the shared content, including project sections and ordered walkthrough steps. Bundled JSON provides the initial content; a configured Supabase store can supply newer published content. Updating the source and publishing CMS content are separate release steps.

sections.heading: Making the terminal useful
sections.body:
The terminal has a virtual filesystem built from the portfolio content. Commands such as ls, cd, cat, and grep let visitors move around and read it; help and man explain what is available.

The fx and scene commands control a live 3D backdrop. It uses easy-3dkit as an installed package, giving the library a real consumer outside its own documentation site.

sections.heading: Keeping the first page light
sections.body:
The 3D code is loaded through the terminal’s lazy backdrop. Forcing those dependencies into a named vendor chunk had pulled them into the entry graph, so I left that part of chunking to the bundler.

The service worker also avoids precaching the heavy backdrop. Otherwise it would download the code at install time even for someone who only wanted the CV.

sections.heading: Making updates manageable
sections.body:
The app starts with bundled content and can hydrate from Supabase. An authenticated editor handles project copy, media, and other site content; saved history supports recovery.

The case studies now include visual walkthroughs and full-size image viewing. The aim is to let someone understand a project before asking them to read the implementation details.

research.title: Cascaded AI Task Decomposition (CATD)
research.summary: A generalizable design pattern for multi-stage computer vision pipelines, validated on bi-scriptual Nepali license-plate recognition.
research.citation: Gajurel, R. K., Sigdel, A., Magar, B. T., & Thapa, S. (2026). Cascaded AI Task Decomposition: A Generalizable Framework for Multi-Stage Computer Vision Pipeline Validated on Automatic Number Plate Recognition for Nepali License Plates. National College of Computer Studies Research Journal, 5(1), 137-167.
highlights: Achieved 97.1% mAP@50 plate localization and 97.8% mAP@50 character recognition using custom-trained YOLOv11n and RT-DETR Base on 61-class bi-scriptual Nepali plates.
Built a two-dimensional cross-domain training strategy (1,380 Nepali + 1,127 Indian plates) enabling compositional zero-shot transfer (+24.5 pp improvement).
Engineered a three-stage cascaded pipeline (YOLOv8n → YOLOv11n → RT-DETR) reaching 90.4% end-to-end precision with 61%-73% compute reduction via intelligent vehicle gating.
Integrated the system as the computer-vision backbone of a smart-parking platform handling automated billing and real-time traffic analytics.
